answer:
(a) Judge refusal is known, not new. GuidedBench motivates its evaluator design partly by letting users pick less safety-restricted judges, 'thus ensuring evaluators do not refuse evaluation tasks involving harmful content' (Sec 5.2), but it prints no evaluator-refusal rate; its measured result is a 76.03-88.28% cut in inter-evaluator variance [1]. AdvPrefix adds affirmative prefilling to its judge 'to handle sensitive content' [9]. 2609.10594 compares six evaluators with human labels: StrongReject reaches 89.5% accuracy / 89.8% F1 / 8.4% FPR, JADES does best, and grader refusal is never discussed [2]. JailJudge reports GPT-4-judge F1 of 55% in complex scenarios [8]; StrongREJECT prints no grader-refusal number [10]. Our contribution is therefore a per-judge x framing quantification on a fixed 60+60 calibration set.

(b) No incumbent is comparable to a parent-free, leave-one-lineage-out, few-prompt screen. AMS's r=-0.546 (p=.043, n=14) is in-sample; its 71% (10/14) holds out only the threshold [11]. RAS needs a per-family reference model, a calibration set and measured ASR [12]. Skin-Deep needs the base model and prints no coefficient (n=7, qualitative) [13]. N-GLARE needs 7000+ trajectories and has no cross-model headline tau [14]. The only genuine cross-family holdout, Hurtado's audit (AUROC 0.95; LOFO balanced accuracy 0.89), needs a parent checkpoint and is a binary abliteration detector [19]. Leong, Li and Labunets are per-model/single-lineage [15, 16, 17]; HRCI is disclaimed as 'not a safety score' [18].

(c) OR-Bench is a single-turn benchmark (80K / 1K hard / 600 toxic prompts) [3]; cited Kaushik2025 is unrelated [4]. TAR resists gradient fine-tuning attacks and never tests training-free edits [5]. Arditi shows erasing one direction removes refusal and adding it induces refusal [6], so a SafeRL shift in a different direction inside a shared subspace is consistent with Arditi; for the multi-direction view see [7].

(d) As of 2026-09-21, 15/36 panel checkpoints have any safety number and 0 are covered by any safety leaderboard; TrustLLM covers mostly 7B+/API models [43]. Of the 15, 6 numbers come from the developer's own reports [24, 25, 33], 6 only from third-party tables [39], and 3 are community self-reports [35, 36, 38]; other abliterated cards print only capability [37]. SafeRL's numbers are not independent: Qwen3Guard was its reward [22, 23]. Capability coverage: MMLU 17, GSM8K 9, Arena-Hard 8 [20, 21, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 34]; sealed Granite/StableLM families publish no size-specific safety table [40, 41], and TrustLLM's leaderboard lists no panel model [42].

(e) Kill-check: nothing kills C1/C2/C5; Report 74's rho=-0.003 (n=16) stays the adverse prior [50] and C5's nearest miss predicts ablation effect, not benchmarks [49]. Content-free steers move refusal like real ones, most strongly below 10B, so C1 must be net of a random steer [44]. Decoy edits can fool DIM-based C2/C5 [45]. Other hits are adjacent [46, 47, 48]. Confidence: high for (a)-(c); medium for (d) (gated/JS pages).

Per judge x framing, how much of the 1,1,1 mass on the 60 known-compliant items is grader refusal versus rubric misreading, and does affirmative prefilling (AdvPrefix-style) remove it?

Can the 6 developer-own safety numbers and the 5-7 over-refusal numbers serve as an external anchor (n<=7) for even a sign test of the top metrics, or is the in-house two-refusal-rate fallback the only viable ground truth?

positioning.grader_refusal: That LLM judges sometimes refuse, or degenerate into a uniform score, when grading responses to harmful prompts under a StrongREJECT-style rubric \citep{Souly2024} is not a new observation: \citet{Huang2025} motivate GuidedEval partly by letting users pick evaluators that are less restrictive in safety constraints, "thus ensuring evaluators do not refuse evaluation tasks involving harmful content," and \citet{Zhu2024} add affirmative prefilling to their judge "to handle sensitive content". What is new here is not the existence of grader-side refusal but its quantification: for two judges (gpt-5-mini, gemini-2.5-flash) crossed with each rubric framing, we measure how often the grader itself refuses or degenerates, directly on a 60 known-compliant + 60 known-refusal calibration set where the ground-truth label is fixed in advance. We do not claim that published StrongREJECT evaluations overestimated safety; a literal all-ones (1,1,1) rubric output is also the rubric's correct, legitimate score for a genuine victim-model refusal, so any headline number must first separate that legitimate case from true grader failure -- which is precisely what our per-judge x framing adjudication contributes.
positioning.incumbents: Existing cheap, white-box safety metrics fall into two groups, neither of which is a parent-free, leave-one-lineage-out, few-prompt, per-checkpoint screen validated against benchmark safety. The first needs a reference: \citet{Lee2026}'s Skin-Deep fragility score contrasts an aligned model against its own base checkpoint; \citet{Huang2026}'s RAS needs a per-family reference model plus a calibration set with other models' measured ASR, and states explicitly that raw scores are not cross-family comparable; \citet{Hurtado2026}'s two-signal audit reaches AUROC 0.95 and a genuine leave-one-family-out balanced accuracy of 0.89, but only by anchoring to a reference checkpoint per family, and only for a binary abliteration label. The second is parent-free but not predictive: \citet{Messenger2026}'s AMS holds out only its classification threshold (71\%, 10/14) while its headline behavioral correlation (r=-0.546, p=.043, n=14) is in-sample; \citet{Lin2026}'s N-GLARE needs 7000+ offline trajectories and reports rank-correlation robustness, not a cross-model headline; and \citet{Lan2026}'s HRCI is explicitly disclaimed by its own authors as "not a safety score." Cross-model regressions such as \citet{Li2026}'s per-model steering slope and \citet{Leong2025}'s template-region NIE are fit in-sample per model, with no held-out lineage.
positioning.ecosystem: As of 2026-09-21, 15 of the 36 sub-4B checkpoints in our panel carry any published safety number, and none of those numbers comes from a dedicated safety leaderboard: HELM Safety, AIR-Bench, SALAD-Bench and TrustLLM list none of the 36, and we found no JailbreakBench or HarmBench entry for any of them. Six of the 15 are the developer's own report or card (Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-4B-SafeRL, the latter evaluated by the team that trained it; Gemma-2-2B-it \citep{Riviere2024}; Phi-4-mini and Phi-3.5-mini \citep{Abouelenin2025}; OLMo-2-1B). Six appear only as baseline rows in another vendor's or a third-party table \citep{Abouelenin2025,Deniz2025}. The remaining three are self-reported by community fine-tuners on their own cards. Only 5 of 36 have an XSTest-style over-refusal number (7 if WildJailbreak benign-prompt refusal is counted). Capability numbers are commoner but harness-dependent: MMLU-family 17/36, GSM8K 9/36, developer-run Arena-Hard 8/36, Open LLM Leaderboard v2 8/36. None of the 15 community fine-tunes (abliterated, CensorTune, SafeRLHF variants) has an independently measured safety number. The checkpoints a downloader actually meets are, as a rule, unmeasured. This is the gap a parent-free, few-prompt score is meant to fill.

citation_fixes.problem: Arditi et al. (2406.11717) support exactly two claims, verified from the abstract: (1) erasing a single found direction from residual-stream activations PREVENTS refusal on harmful instructions (removal claim, underlies abliteration), and (2) ADDING that direction ELICITS refusal even on harmless instructions (induction claim). Both are about a single model's OWN refusal direction found by contrastive activation differences; Arditi never claims that two DIFFERENT interventions (e.g. SafeRL fine-tuning vs. abliteration) must move along the SAME direction. Our Step-1 finding (SHARED_SUBSPACE_DIFFERENT_DIRECTIONS: first principal angle 31.1 deg vs. anisotropy-matched null, mean-shift cosine -0.09 at the null, max |cos| 0.20 vs. null p95 0.41, positive control abliterated-vs-abliterated 0.885 vs. null 0.750) is therefore CONSISTENT with, not a refutation of, Arditi: abliteration removes the refusal direction by construction (that IS Arditi's mechanism), so a differently-trained intervention (SafeRL) landing in the same low-dimensional subspace but along a different direction inside it is the expected pattern, not evidence against a single-direction account. For the multi-direction nuance we instead cite Joad2026 (arXiv 2602.02132, verified title 'There Is More to Refusal in Large Language Models than a Single Direction', EMNLP 2026), whose abstract explicitly shows refusal categories correspond to geometrically distinct directions that nonetheless act as a 'shared one-dimensional control knob' under linear steering -- directly analogous to our shared-subspace-different-directions finding.
citation_fixes.corrected_text: Arditi et al. show that a single direction, when erased from a model's residual stream, prevents refusal on harmful instructions, and, when added, elicits refusal on harmless ones \citep{Arditi2024}. Our Step-1 result -- SafeRL and abliteration share a low-dimensional subspace (first principal angle 31.1$^\circ$ vs. the anisotropy-matched null) but move along different directions within it (mean-shift cosine -0.09, at the sign-flip null; max $|\cos|$ 0.20 vs. null $p_{95}$ 0.41; positive control, abliterated-vs-abliterated, at 0.885 vs. null 0.750) -- is consistent with, not a refutation of, \citet{Arditi2024}: abliteration removes the refusal direction by construction, so an independently-trained intervention landing in the same subspace along a different direction is expected, not evidence that a single direction is an oversimplification. For the multi-direction view we instead follow \citet{Joad2026}, who show refusal categories occupy geometrically distinct directions that nonetheless behave as a shared linear control knob under steering.
citation_fixes.quote: we show that refusal is mediated by a one-dimensional subspace ... we find a single direction such that erasing this direction from the model's residual stream activations prevents it from refusing harmful instructions, while adding this direction elicits refusal on even harmless instructions.

hits.title: Steering Interference Reflects the Model's Defaults, Not the Behavior Directions
hits.quote: A direction carrying no behavioral content, matched to a real steer only in the size of the vector it adds, moves the same behaviors in the same order as real steers do (rank correlation 0.90)
hits.quote2: the pull toward defaults strongest below 10B parameters and weakening in each family's largest
hits.why: Any steer (including a norm-matched contentless one) pulls sub-10B models toward refusal; a harm-to-refusal gain measured by steering is therefore confounded by a generic 'roll toward defaults' term that is largest exactly in our sub-4B regime. C1 must be reported NET of a norm-matched random-direction steer at the same layer (our iter-2 ROSI hidden-direction control already showed ~0.04 D2 from a non-refusal direction). Does not correlate anything with benchmark safety, so does not kill.

hits.title: Decoy Direction Optimization: A Post-Hoc Defense Against LLM Abliteration (Muhamed, Diab, Smith)
hits.quote: ablation attacks rely on contrastive estimators to find the refusal direction ... the decoy corrupts their estimator, tricking them into ablating a harmless orthogonal feature while the actual safety mechanism remains intact
hits.why: Shows a cheap post-hoc weight edit that decouples the difference-in-means direction from the causal refusal subspace across six families. Any parent-free score that estimates the refusal direction by DIM (C2 self-ablation sensitivity; C5 weight-path gain onto the DIM direction) can be deliberately fooled: a DDO-hardened model would show low self-ablation sensitivity / misattributed gain while remaining safe. Adds an adversarial-robustness limitation and a natural stress-test checkpoint; it is a defense paper, not a metric-vs-benchmark correlation.

hits.title: Refusal Reads Only a Slice of What the Model Knows: Harm-Keyed Routing and Its Exceptions Across Model Families
hits.quote: Across four open-weight models spanning three families ... The central result is causal and comes from one model, OLMo-3.
hits.why: Measures what refusal reads (harm vs moral subspace) by interchange on 4 models (7B-20B); the causal result is single-model; no per-model score is correlated with a safety benchmark. Cite as evidence that harm-to-refusal routing differs by family (Llama reads broad moral content, Qwen unresolved) - a mechanistic reason C1 may not transfer across families.

hits.title: The Role of Fine-grained Harm Signals in LLM Safety (Park, Jeong, Kim, Oh; KAIST)
hits.quote: Whether category residuals induce refusal also varies across categories, but this category-wise pattern is more model-dependent.
hits.why: Steering category residuals induces refusal with model-dependent strength on 3 models (Gemma-2-9B-IT, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct); no correlation of that per-model strength with any benchmark. Supports the premise that harm-to-refusal gain varies per model; cite, does not scoop.

hits.title: HARC: Coupling Harmfulness and Refusal Directions for Robust Safety Alignment
hits.quote: Prompt-side decoupling varies across families, where Llama and Gemma show the cleanest separation while Mistral and Qwen exhibit more entangled prompt-side directions.
hits.why: Characterises harmfulness-refusal geometry across five architectures and uses it for a defense; grep for 'correlat' found no per-model score correlated with benchmark safety (4 matches, none a correlation). Missed by the iter-3 check; add to related work.

hits.why: Per-PROMPT harmfulness moderator (F1 vs guard models), not a per-MODEL safety score.
